title: Seven in every moment
hookLine: contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life, attention: present in every mind-moment

cards: A king once asked a monk to do something impossible. The king was Milinda, the monk was Nagasena, and their long conversation was written down as the Questions of King Milinda.
Nagasena had been naming what happens in the mind in a single moment: contact, feeling, perception, intention, and more. So the king pushed. Can you pull them apart?
Show me this one here, and that one over there. Nagasena answered him with a kitchen.

teach.b: Suppose, he said, the royal cook makes a sauce with curds and salt and ginger and pepper. If the king said, bring me just the taste of the salt, could the cook do it? No.
Every flavor is really there, each with its own character, but none can be lifted out alone.
The Abhidhammattha Sangaha names seven mental factors present in every moment of consciousness, whatever kind it is: kind or cruel, sharp or sleepy.
Contact, phassa: the mind meets its object, like two hands meeting in a clap. Feeling, vedana: that meeting has a tone, pleasant, unpleasant, or neither.
Perception, sanna: the object is recognized and marked, this is blue, this is my sister's voice. Intention, cetana: the mind leans and organizes, aiming somewhere.

One-pointedness: it rests on one object, even for an instant. The life faculty: what keeps the others going for as long as the moment lasts. And attention, manasikara: the mind turned toward this rather than that.
Seven, in a moment of reading a street sign, a moment of anger, a moment of compassion. That's what makes the list useful.

teach.h: ALWAYS A TONE, ALWAYS A LEAN.
teach.b: Feeling is in every moment, so no moment is without some tone. Intention is in every moment, so the mind is always leaning somewhere, even when it seems idle.
And attention is always pointed, so the question is never whether the mind is attending, only to what. The sauce can't be separated in the bowl.

teach.h: NAMED, SO MORE CAN BE TASTED.
teach.b: The Abhidhamma names its parts anyway, not to take the sauce apart, but so more of it can be tasted.

how: Abhidhamma students learn the seven universal factors by their Pali names, and some insight meditation teachers ask students to notice contact and the tone of feeling, pleasant, unpleasant or neutral, as it arises.

games.q: what does “seven in every moment” mean?
o: factors present in every moment of mind, kind or cruel
the seven daily times a monk sits to meditate
seven stages a meditator passes on the way to calm

s: the seven factors appear only in calm, wholesome moments
the manual finds them in every moment of consciousness: kind or cruel, sharp or sleepy.
Nagasena compares the factors in a moment to the flavors in a sauce
every flavor is there, but no one can lift out just the salt.
here, feeling means an emotion like sadness
vedana here is the tone of a moment: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither.

games.q: you're the royal cook. the king asks for only the taste of the salt from a finished sauce. what do you do?
o: strain the sauce until only the salt is left.
say it can't be done: the flavors are mixed.
bring him a spoonful of plain salt instead.
games.why: in the Questions of King Milinda, Nagasena says the cook couldn't do it. each flavor is real and distinct, and none comes out alone. the factors in a moment are like that.

practice: If you'd like, rest one hand on your knee or a table and notice the moment it touches, contact, and the tone that comes with it: pleasant, unpleasant or neither.

Lift it and set it down again, then try the same with a sound in the room, and with the breath at the nostrils. Just two things each time, it touched and it had a tone; the other five are there whether you find them or not.

wordCard.voice: Seven in every moment. Contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life and attention: the factors the manual finds in every moment of mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali phassa: contact, the first of the seven factors in every moment.

carryVoice: Your line: seven always. Always a tone, always a lean, even in an idle moment. Go gently.

sources.ref: Abhidhammattha Sangaha, ch. 2 (the seven universal mental factors)
Milindapanha II.3 (the cook's sauce: separating the mental qualities; Rhys Davids, SBE XXXV, 1890)
